https://www.politico.eu/article/6-issues.text: Ursula von der Leyen has three years left to cement her legacy, but it’ll be far from easy. Von der Leyen’s second term ends in 2029, by which time she’ll have been at the helm of the European Commission for a decade. If, as Brussels Playbook reported earlier this summer, the EU executive chief won’t seek a third term, then she’s in the final stretch of her career in Brussels. Her time in office has been dominated by crisis management — Covid-19, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, sky-high energy prices, war in Gaza. In the years to come, the challenges will likely keep mounting, including competition from China and the United States, and upcoming elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland that could reshape the EU. Advertisement In the Commission’s Berlaymont HQ, von der Leyen and her team are feverishly working on her State of the EU speech, to be delivered on Sept. 16. It’s when she will set out her plan for the years to come. After that, she’ll have to deliver. “Speeches are important. But it’s the actions that create legacy,” said Martin Hojsík, a vice president of the European Parliament from the Renew Europe group. “Europe has become more vulnerable economically, competitiveness remains a major challenge, social and regional inequalities persist, and too often her Commission has reacted to crises rather than anticipated them,” said Victor Negrescu, a Parliament vice president from the Socialists and Democrats group. “I expect her to use this moment to defend her record, but also to explain how Europe can deliver more on growth, investment, social cohesion and strategic autonomy. For me, the real question is not how her legacy is presented, but what concrete results Europeans will see by the end of this mandate.” Here are six potential headaches likely to define von der Leyen’s remaining time in office. 1. Reversing Europe’s decline Will von der Leyen be able to stem the Continent’s economic decline … or oversee the death of its industrial heartlands? It was von der Leyen who asked former Italian PM and European Central Bank chief Mario Draghi to draw up a report into the continent’s competitiveness. He was brutal in his assessment , saying that “without action, we will have to either compromise our welfare, our environment or our freedom.” He called on Europe to invest an additional €800 billion a year to drag itself out of a trough of low productivity and feeble growth that’s pushing it behind the U.S. and China in the international pecking order. Advertisement Von der Leyen promised to turn Draghi’s warning into an industrial strategy, but the headwinds are strong. European companies face high energy prices, fragmented capital markets, complex regulation and intensifying competition from abroad. And while European companies need Chinese markets and supply chains, that dependency comes at a high cost. State subsidies have allowed Chinese firms to build capacity that far exceeds domestic demand, and their EVs, batteries, solar panels and steel are putting pressure on EU rivals. Meanwhile, Beijing’s stranglehold over critical minerals used in the green transition and high-tech sectors creates vast danger. “What you have seen with the EU position on relations with China is the status quo is far too heavily tilted in China’s favor and cannot endure,” said a Commission official, granted anonymity to speak freely. “At EU level, there’s now near-total agreement on diagnosing the problems. There is near-total agreement on what the solutions are to address those problems. The only remaining question is how robust are member states willing to be in their follow-through.” Mario Draghi smiles after being awarded the 2026 International Charlemagne Prize of Aachen, on May 14, 2026. | Sascha Schuermann/AFP via Getty Images Von der Leyen’s dilemma is how to keep the Chinese market open while preventing overcapacity from hollowing out EU industry. The Commission is overseeing a reset in China relations , while considering stronger trade-defense tools and measures to reduce supply-chain dependence. It’s a delicate balance: too much confrontation could trigger a damaging trade war; too little could leave Europe without a viable industrial base. Brussels and Beijing are engaged in talks to resolve the issue. Trade chief Maroš Šefčovič has set an October deadline to make progress. Failure could mean that China becomes the next front in the trade war. Advertisement 2. Protecting EU regulations from Trump Can von der Leyen rein in Big Tech without every European decision on competition, data, digital sovereignty or child safety becoming a transatlantic confrontation? The Digital Markets Act and Digital Services Act are in their enforcement phase, and the EU’s fines against Apple , Meta and Google have already infuriated Washington . Von der Leyen is pushing ahead with plans to restrict children under 13 from using social media, which could provoke Donald Trump further. “We would not presume to tell the U.S. how to regulate on their sovereign territory. And that is the very fair and coherent thing we ask for in return,” said the Commission official quoted above. 3. Addressing the climate crisis while slashing green rules The Green Deal was the defining project of von der Leyen’s first term. But with far-right forces surging around the EU and an outcry that green rules are adding to Europe’s industrial strain, von der Leyen is now being forced to undo the very policies she implemented . Farmers have hit the streets of Europe ; industry and governments are demanding simplification. But Europe is facing extreme heat waves , wildfires, and worsening climate risks that make environmental action more urgent than ever. If von der Leyen weakens the Green Deal too much, she risks losing credibility with citizens and her coalition partners. If she insists on ambitious rules, she could provoke more political backlash. Advertisement “Some environmental policies were adopted without thinking about the social issues,” acknowledged Marie Toussaint, a French Green MEP. “How to heat your home? For some people the bills are already impossible to pay. So we need to ensure that in every sector we have this social concern and we refrain from adopting anything that would worsen people’s lives.” 4. Defending Europe and Ukraine Europe’s security debate has moved from speeches about “strategic autonomy” to the urgent question of where to get weapons and deter Russian President Vladimir Putin. The EU is increasing defense spending, backing joint procurement and trying to expand industrial capacity through initiatives such as the €150 billion SAFE program. But national governments still disagree over how much to spend and how to spend it. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, flanked by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, delivers a speech during a ceremony to mark the Day of Ukrainian Statehood, in Kyiv on July 15, 2026. | Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP via Getty Images The test is whether Europe can build a defense industry that can stand on its own, given the Trump administration’s repeated undermining of NATO. Von der Leyen will also need to ensure that Ukraine enters any potential peace negotiations with Russia in the best position possible. “We know exactly how to talk to Russians,” said Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna. “Pressure, no compromises, and only from [a position of] strength.” Advertisement That means von der Leyen must ensure Ukraine gets financial and military support as well as credible long-term security guarantees, while keeping the Trump administration onside. But while in Brussels support for Ukraine remains high, more Kremlin-friendly governments have won power around the EU, with the potential for others to join them after a series of elections in 2027, including in France and Italy. “We operate in the real world. We have to take political reality and political developments into account in the work we do,” said the Commission official. Regardless, they added, “President von der Leyen will continue to make the case for Ukraine because that’s clearly in Europe’s best interest.” 5. Expanding the EU Ukraine, Moldova and countries in the Western Balkans have moved closer to the EU, but political support for enlargement is not the same as readiness to admit new members. Candidate countries must still complete difficult reforms on the rule of law, corruption and judicial independence. Current EU members worry about the cost of enlargement, future funding needs and whether the institutions can function with more than 30 members. But von der Leyen needs to show that accession is still a credible process rather than a permanently postponed promise, before the countries in the EU’s waiting room run out of patience and look elsewhere for alliances. Advertisement “We deserve to be in a much more advanced position than we are right now,” North Macedonia’s Foreign Minister Timčo Mucunski said about his country’s stalled bid to join the EU. “To say that we have been treated unfairly is an understatement.” 6. Paying for it all The EU’s next long-term budget will determine which of these headaches von der Leyen can actually treat. The Commission proposed an almost €2 trillion budget for 2028–2034 , but two entrenched camps are battling over the plan. The so-called Friends of Cohesion — among them Italy, Greece, Poland and Spain — want more money for traditional spending areas, particularly cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy , and want those funds delivered through familiar national and regional channels. The other camp, made up of frugal countries including Germany, Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands, wants less spending and a different allocation of cash: more for innovation, defense and European industrial capacity. The fight collides with the political calendar. Advertisement A cadre of the EU’s biggest countries will hold elections in 2027, including France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Some politicians will be reluctant to explain to voters why they should send more money to Brussels; others why traditional funding should be reduced. Yet the new EU budget (known as the Multiannual Financial Framework) must take effect on Jan. 1, 2028. That means the deal needs to be negotiated well in advance. Von der Leyen’s second term ends in 2029. | Olivier Matthys/EPA The closer it gets to 2027, the more domestic politics will dominate the talks — and the harder it will be to secure unanimity in the Council and consent from the European Parliament. “When it comes to MFF negotiations, endgame negotiations are always tough, but it always gets done,” said the Commission official. “Those exact motivations [2027 elections] are fantastic factors to get the job done now.” Eliza Gkritsi, Seb Starcevic, Max Griera and Mathieu Pollet contributed to this story. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: In some diplomatic circles, there are concerns that the diesel deal ‘is only the visible tip of the iceberg’, says career diplomat Nigel Gould-Davies, with the White House privately pivoting towards a ‘much more substantial’ pro-Russia tilt. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP View image in fullscreen In some diplomatic circles, there are concerns that the diesel deal ‘is only the visible tip of the iceberg’, says career diplomat Nigel Gould-Davies, with the White House privately pivoting towards a ‘much more substantial’ pro-Russia tilt. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP First Edition newsletter World news Thursday briefing: Thanks to an erratic Trump, peace in Ukraine is still far away In today’s newsletter: As Russia resists a ceasefire and Trump’s shifting priorities unsettle allies, an end to the conflict isn’t getting any closer Michael Segalov Thu 15 Oct 2026 01.44 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. In his usual asinine unconventional approach to international relations, Donald Trump announced on Sunday (via Truth Social, how else) an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine”, apparently without checking with either side. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said any such deal was “news to me,” nonetheless declared he was “ready and we will accept it”. Vladimir Putin responded by blowing up some Ukrainian power plants. This has been the tenor of much diplomacy during Trump’s tenure: false starts, U-turns, incoherent positions (and some playful flirting with Vlad). Meanwhile fighting continues, and America’s allies attempt to manage the fallout. Andy Burnham hosted Zelenskyy at Downing Street yesterday, stating the UK is doubling down on its support for Ukraine, and pointedly calling on others to “follow suit”. It’s a negotiator’s nightmare. So how are ambassadors, spooks and diplomats handling the chaos? Is an actual ceasefire or peace deal within their grasp? For today’s First Edition, I spoke to career diplomat and former ambassador Nigel Gould-Davies to find out. Before that, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories UK | Sally Rooney has said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for the banned organisation Palestine Action. Gaza | Israel is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned. EU | Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said . Ukraine | Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to immediately halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry. Vaccine | Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said. In depth: ‘A peace agreement is only possible when both sides believe that it better serves their interests’ View image in fullscreen Ukrainian rescuers work at the site of a Russian strike on a residential building in Kharkiv. Photograph: Sergey Kozlov/EPA Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, efforts to secure either a temporary ceasefire or a permanent peace deal have resolutely failed. Endless rounds of talks in Belarus, Turkey, Abu Dhabi and Geneva have all proved futile. To Nigel Gould-Davies, it’s obvious why. A former British diplomat, he was head of economics at the Foreign Office in Moscow before his stint as the UK’s ambassador to Belarus. Today, he is senior fellow for Russia and Eurasia at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. Gould-Davies tells me that there are established norms for negotiating during military conflicts. Diplomats look for the interests, needs and red lines that each side articulates, in pursuit of the elusive “win set”. “A peace agreement is only possible when both sides believe that it better serves their interests to end the fighting than to continue,” he says. “You have to find that overlap in the Venn diagram that leads to a defined set of conditions which, despite involving painful compromises, is ultimately judged to better serve each side than continuing to fight. “The problem with this situation is that Russia has no interest in ending the war,” he says. Tricky to find common ground, then. It is through this lens that we should view all Russia-Ukraine talks since Trump’s return to the presidency, Gould-Davies suggests. “They have not really been negotiations,” but “parallel efforts by Russia and Ukraine to persuade the White House it’s the other side’s fault” that a peace agreement (and, perhaps more importantly to Trump, that elusive Nobel peace prize) had failed to materialise. That said, the respective red lines aren’t difficult to identify. Ukraine has time and again said it is willing to accept an unconditional ceasefire . “Russia, by contrast, has repeatedly said publicly that it is not interested in a ceasefire,” says Gould-Davies, only in a full and final end to the war that, in Russian terms, means “decisive superiority and dominance over a severely weakened Ukraine”. That’s an outcome Ukraine can’t, and won’t, sign up for. The ‘non-standard president’ This is already a headache for UK, European and American diplomats, who most recently met in Miami at the end of last week. But there’s also the added Trump-shaped impediment to grapple with; what Gould-Davies diplomatically describes as the challenge of having “a non-standard president” in the White House. When Trump unilaterally declared an energy ceasefire, Gould-Davies says, it had “no basis whatsoever in reality”. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv was aware. “He simply made it up … a product of a fantasy.” The botched digital diplomacy aside, Trump’s interests also don’t appear aligned with Ukraine or traditional US allies. “[Trump’s] natural centre of gravity is to favour Russia,” says Gould-Davies, citing restrictions on US weapons supplies and past pauses in intelligence sharing. Yesterday, Zelenskyy accused Trump of restricting Ukrainian access to “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defences. Granted, Trump has at times sided with the Ukrainian president: sanctioning Russian oil companies and helping Ukraine target Russian energy infrastructure. But for all Trump’s “lurching”, says Gould-Davies, his theory of ending the war involves concessions to Russia and coercion of Ukraine. The price of a deal After a period of relative quiet from Trump on the Russia-Ukraine front, this week Trump’s attention returned. With Americans facing soaring energy costs, he announced a plan to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down pump prices, much to the dismay not just of European leaders but a bipartisan group of US senators, too. Leave aside, for a second, suggestions that these imports could be illegal under American law and that quantities being discussed are seemingly too small to actually affect prices , even if the fuel could reach the US ahead of next month’s midterms, as Trump hopes. In some diplomatic circles, there are concerns that the diesel deal “is only the visible tip of the iceberg”, says Gould-Davies, with the White House privately pivoting towards a “much more substantial” pro-Russia tilt. Gould-Davies suspects that Trump could be, via Russia, seeking to get Iran to ease the blockade on the strait of Hormuz, in the hope of actually bringing down fuel prices before American voters head to the polls. Putin’s quid pro quo for brokering these efforts, Gould-Davies says, “could be an easing of America’s sanctions on Russia and an ending to America’s support for Ukraine”. It’s just a theory, he caveats, “but join the dots and it logically makes sense”. Either way, for diplomats it’s just further proof that Trump’s mercurial methods are more a hindrance than help. The quiet work behind the scenes Nonetheless, diplomatic back channels remain operational: secret, closed-door meetings and off-the-record communications between all sides. Not that Gould-Davies thinks they’re worth the effort. “There is a degree of collective delusion here,” he says: “A hope that Russia can somehow be persuaded” to change course, for which “there is literally no evidence for that whatsoever”. He worries that these informal discussions could even be “actively unhelpful, because they perpetuate the illusion that peace may be around the corner”. And, while Europe might traditionally have focused its diplomatic efforts in hostile territory, attention has now turned towards the US itself. There’s still hope that Trump’s whispers might pay further dividends. As Gould-Davies puts it, this “ Avengers assemble ” approach has seen European leaders and diplomats descend on Washington when Trump’s veered too far off course. For all the tumult, he says, this has proved effective in averting “the nightmare scenario” of Trump binning off America’s old transatlantic partners for good. But as fans of Netflix’s The Diplomat will know, even diplomacy between allies isn’t plain sailing. “Right now even ‘the White House’ is an abstraction,” says Gould-Davies. “It consists of many different players, plenty of whom have different views privately from President Trump.” Take John Ratcliffe, director of the CIA, who visited Moscow this summer. There is “reliable speculation”, says Gould-Davies, that he hoped to “warn Russia against escalation into Europe”. It’s a totally different note to those currently being struck by Trump. “There are people in positions of power and influence still in this administration who understand the problem of Russia in the right way,” says Gould-Davies. With that in mind, western diplomats will continue to try to shift the balance of influences within the White House, but they’re reliant on what he labels a White House Kremlinology – “trying to understand the different views and moods of those around Trump and who will be the last person to whisper in his ear.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen How We Win, a new Guardian newsletter on defeating Trumpism. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian Champions League | Paris Saint-Germain romped to a 4-2 victory over Manchester City, while Bradley Barcola hit his first Liverpool goals with a hat-trick in a 6-3 win over Lask. Elsewhere, Aston Villa demolished Fenerbahce 6-0 at Villa Park. Fifa | Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over the aborted World Cup sell-off plan, the Folarin Balogun affair and awarding Donald Trump the Fifa peace prize at what is expected to be a heated meeting on Thursday. Formula One | Formula One has confirmed Rwanda will join its calendar , ­having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a ­purpose-built ­circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. The front pages View image in fullscreen 2026-10-15-dde6e8 Photograph: The Guardian The Guardian splashes on “Zelenskyy blames Trump for loss of protection from Russian raids”. The Times has “Zelensky: My people will die after Trump betrayal”, the Telegraph runs “More on benefits at age seven than age 50” and top story at the Financial Times is “Jump in US inflation deepens pain for voters ahead of key midterm elections”. Elsewhere, focus is on the Russell Brand trial. Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. Reporting the prosecution’s opening statement, the Sun headlines with the quote “‘Ruthless calculated sexual predator’”, The i Paper also headlines with “Brand a ‘ruthless and calculated sexual predator’”, the Mail has “The ‘predator’ in sunglasses” and The Mirror leads with the quote “‘Predator’”. The Latest View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian. India’s Cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown A fresh wave of protests by India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has been met with a brutal crackdown by Narendra Modi’s government and the closure of a historic protest site in Delhi. Two of the movement’s leaders have been imprisoned for five days for violating suppression measures. The protests, which began over frustration about education and unemployment, are now focused on voting rights. Modi’s government denies claims that it is seeking to disenfranchise millions of voters. But its treatment of protesters has been criticised by the UN and Amnesty International and raised concerns that the country is sliding further into autocracy. Lucy Hough speaks to the south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen – watch on YouTube Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings View image in fullscreen Illustration: Nicola Jennings/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen Hive of activity … Aref Haboo (left), Bybi’s principal beekeeper, with Mohamed, a fellow apiarist. Photograph: Valdemar Ren/The Guardian On Copenhagen’s rooftops live 80 to 100 colonies of honeybees, tended by a collective of beekeepers called Bybi. Set up in 2010 with the aim of employing marginalised people, Bybi’s work has evolved into a response to the modern economic system. With the help of volunteers, from refugees to people on incapacity benefits, they produce between four and six tonnes of honey every year, which they sell (often letting people pay what they like) or give away, asking that people share it with loved ones and plant a flower to help the bees. They also run schools programmes, supported by sponsorships from universities and corporations. “Bybi is a constellation of time, work, money, community and connection,” says founder Oliver Maxwell, “asking an open question: what would it take for bees, people and communities to thrive?” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/23/oil-.text: The United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill from a tanker off its coast on Friday, as numerous vessels in Gulf waters came under attack in the ongoing Iran war.The authorities "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement, referring to an emirate north of Dubai.It said "teams immediately began containment, cordoning, clean-up and remediation... to limit environmental impacts", adding that the emirate's beaches had been closed.Many residents in the country's north have reported unusual oil-like smells on social media in recent days, including in northern districts of Dubai.Frequent attacks on ships have been reported in recent weeks near the Strait of Hormuz, control of which remains at the heart of the war between Iran and the US.The maritime security agency UKMTO reported on 9 October that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control.According to maritime security company Vanguard, the vessel was the oil tanker GEM NO.2, sailing under the Panamanian flag.Roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. Both Tehran and Washington have implemented blockades in the strait, while Iran has repeatedly targeted cargo vessels using the southern section of the waterway.Earlier this week, Iran's IRGC said in a statement that it targets tankers trying to use what Tehran unilaterally designates as an unauthorised route through the strait's southern section, near the Omani coast.Tehran has no recognised authority under international maritime law to restrict or authorise passage through Hormuz, which is subject to the right of transit passage under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.The UAE lies close to the Strait of Hormuz, just 40-50 nautical miles from the waterway's narrowest point.
